paragraphs: I don't know whether you'll agree, but few things in this world lift the spirits quite like the rays of the rising sun. Whatever worries weigh on us through the long hours of the night, sunlight drives them away, telling a story of hope and all the possibilities a new day holds.

And that is how our story begins: with a beautiful, joyful sunrise. Its rays bathed the beach in warm, golden light, while a gentle breeze played with the sand, stirring little swirls here and there. The sea, calm now, had washed amber and white seashells ashore during the night. They sparkled in the morning light like tiny stars. And the water itself had traded its usual greens and deep blues for shades of pink and gold.

Near the beach, in a grassy meadow, stood a little mud cottage. It was a humble home belonging to a humble couple. He was a fisherman who went out to sea at dawn each day to catch fish. She looked after the house, the hens, and their little garden of carrots and tomatoes. Though they were poor, they loved each other dearly.

That morning, as always, the fisherman readied his boat and checked his nets before setting out. His wife kissed him goodbye, then stood waving long after the little boat had begun to disappear beyond the horizon.

The sea has a mind of its own. So that day, despite the lovely weather, the fisherman caught nothing all morning. Only in the afternoon, as he hauled in his nets to head for shore, did something land in the bottom of his boat that made him rub his eyes in wonder.
“It cannot be,” he said to himself. “It cannot be.”

In the bottom of his boat lay a little flounder, with eyes on its back and a crooked little mouth. That was ordinary and familiar. What was not ordinary or familiar was the colour of its scales, which shone like real gold coins. It looked more like a jewel than a living creature, yet it flapped in the net like any other sea creature he had caught. The fisherman knelt and freed it from the net, then stroked its golden scales in wonder. And then the little fish spoke in a human voice:
“Kind fisherman, please let me go. I will give you anything your heart desires.”
“Why, little fish, you can speak!” said the astonished fisherman. “How is that possible?”

“No stranger than the colour of my scales. Many creatures swim in the depths that you on land know nothing about,” the fish replied. Then it repeated its plea. “I have the power to grant your heart's desire. Just make a wish and put me back in the water, and I will grant it.”

The fisherman smiled to himself, gently cupped the fish in his hands, and leaned over the side to release it into the sea. It dived beneath the water. Then its golden scales flashed once more near the surface, and it turned towards the boat and asked:
“What about your wish?”
“What could you give me? My strong hands and my small but sturdy boat are all I need in life. Farewell, little golden fish.”
And so the fisherman parted with the flounder and rowed home.

His wife met him on the shore, and together they walked towards their humble cottage. On the way, the fisherman told her about meeting the golden fish. She listened to the whole story in disbelief. When he had finished, she said:
“You were too hasty, husband. That kind creature was our chance of a better life! Look at the way we live. Please go back tomorrow and ask it for a proper house. Do it for us.”
The fisherman fell deep in thought and spent the whole night wondering what to do. At last, he decided to fulfil his wife's wish and find the golden flounder.

The next day's sunrise promised fine weather once again. With the morning waves murmuring around him and a fresh breeze on his face, the fisherman set out to find the golden fish. When he reached the place where he had met it the day before, he leaned over the side and called:
“Golden fish!” Silence answered him. “Golden fish!” The calm sea rocked him in the breeze. “Golden fish!”
Then he heard a splash and saw the flounder, its scales gleaming in the sunlight more beautifully than a king's crown. It was the very same fish.
“Hello, my friend! What brings you here? Have you changed your mind about making a wish?”
“I need nothing for myself, but my wife longs for a new house. Our humble cottage is old now, and it has only one room. Could you perhaps turn it into a proper house, little golden fish?”
“Of course. When you return to shore, you will find a splendid new house where your cottage stood.”
With that, the fish dived back into the sea, and the fisherman rowed towards the beach.

When the fisherman reached the shore, he could hardly believe his eyes. Where their cottage had stood just a few hours before, there now rose a spacious brick house with an upper floor, an attic, and a wide porch. Smoke curled from its stone chimney, and the garden was full not only of vegetables but also of exotic herbs and flowers.
His wife ran out to meet him, smiling broadly.
“Look, husband, what a beautiful house we have! Isn't it something to be happy about?”
“The golden fish truly kept its word. It is a beautiful house. And seeing you happy brings me great joy.”

For a few days, the fisherman and his wife lived in quiet contentment. They tended the hens and the garden and ate what grew beside their home. Their worries vanished like a bursting soap bubble. Yet each day his wife smiled a little less, until at last she said:

“I cannot enjoy this house knowing that the golden fish could have given us so much more. Go out to sea at once, find it, and ask for a manor house. A proper nobleman's manor, with servants and a carriage.”
The fisherman was troubled, but he obeyed his wife. More than anything, he wanted to see her happy.

As he climbed into his boat, he eyed the clouds uneasily. The fine weather was over; now anything might happen. With the morning waves growing louder and a cold wind blowing around him, he set out to find the golden fish. When he reached the place where he had met it before, he leaned over the side and called:
“Golden fish!” The wind answered with a sigh. “Golden fish!” The waves rocked his little boat hard. “Golden fish!”
Then golden scales flashed among the waves, and the flounder surfaced with a splash. Surprised to see the fisherman again, it asked:
“What are you doing here, fisherman? Have you come to talk? How is life in your new house?”

“I am happy, but my wife is sad, and the house no longer brings her joy. She longs for a manor house, with servants and a carriage. I have come to ask you, little golden fish, to turn our house into just such a manor.”
“You spared my life, fisherman. I can grant your wish once more. So be it. When you return to shore, you will find a beautiful manor house where your home stood.”
With that, the fish dived back into the sea, and the fisherman rowed towards the beach.

Back on shore, the fisherman saw a sight beyond all his expectations. Where the pretty seaside house had stood, there now rose a grand manor with whitewashed walls and oak columns supporting a roof over its entrance. Beside it stood farm buildings, a kitchen, and stables, all nestled in a flower-filled garden. A carriage drawn by four horses waited at the double front doors, while servants in matching uniforms bustled about the grounds.

A smile returned to his wife's face. For a few days, at least. But one morning, the fisherman woke at dawn and could not find her anywhere. He searched the whole manor and questioned the servants, until at last he found her in the farthest corner of the garden.

She sat in a summerhouse, gazing at the sea as gusts of wind swept across it. A forced smile appeared on her face, but it did not reach her eyes. There was something both sad and menacing in them. She spoke to the fisherman:

“The golden fish has given us a beautiful manor. It is hard not to enjoy it. Yet I still cannot stop thinking that we have wasted our chance. You must find the fish at once and ask it to make me a queen and turn our manor into a castle.”

The sea was restless. Wind swept across the water, raising tall waves, and black clouds covered the sky. To make matters worse, drizzle began as soon as the fisherman climbed into his boat. Despite the threatening weather, the brave fisherman, who loved his wife dearly, set out and reached the place where the fish lived. Once again, he leaned over the side and called:
“Golden fish!” The restless wind answered him. “Golden fish!” The waves tossed the boat roughly. “Golden fish!”

After his third call, something golden flashed in the depths. The flounder swam beneath the boat and circled it, as though reluctant to surface. The fisherman watched from his boat as the high waves rocked it. Then the fish rose from the water and spoke.
“Oh, fisherman, fisherman. Surely there have been enough visits. Can't you see the sea rebelling? How many more times will your wife's desires disturb the peace of our world?”
“What do you mean, little fish? I have come with just one request. For you, it is such a little thing. And by making my wife happy, you will make me happy too!”
The fish thought for a moment. Then it said, “For the last time, fisherman. What does your wife wish for?”
“She wishes to be a queen and live in a castle. Please, little fish, grant my request.”
“I will grant it. When you return to shore, you will see a castle. Now farewell, and do not come here again.”
The fish dived and vanished into the dark depths of the sea.

It happened just as the fish had said: a magnificent castle stood where the manor had been. Wild waves crashed against foundations carved into the hard rock of the sea cliff. A broad wall crowned with white stone battlements guarded it, and four slender towers with sharp, pointed roofs rose above everything. The only way inside was over a drawbridge, and servants and courtiers in richly decorated liveries bustled everywhere. Only one thing spoiled this majestic sight: the black storm clouds gathering on the horizon.
The fisherman found his wife in the great hall. She sat on a marble throne, holding a golden sceptre. On her head was a crown richly set with emeralds and rubies. He approached, bowed, and asked:
“Wife, are you happy?”
“I am. For now,” she replied in an indifferent voice, without even looking at her husband. “Now go and rest in your chamber. We shall speak another time.”

The fisherman found his chamber among the castle's winding corridors and went inside. Used to a humble life, he could not fall asleep at first in the enormous bed that awaited him. When he finally did, his sleep was troubled by strange dreams and shadowy things he could not quite make out. Outside, a storm raged.
Suddenly, lightning struck nearby, and the fisherman woke with a start. The queen stood at the head of his bed, her face and figure looming in the flashes of lightning behind her.

“Get up, husband. Being a queen is beneath me. You must get into your boat and go out to sea at once! Find the fish again. It must make me a god! I want to rule not a manor, not a kingdom, but the whole world!”
Terrified, the fisherman looked at the terrible storm raging outside.
“My dear wife, there is a storm!”
“No excuses. I will not wait! Go out to sea, or I shall have you thrown into the dungeon this very day!”

Once again, the fisherman set out across the raging sea to find the fish. The gale blew without pause, while black clouds and heavy rain made it hard to see or steer. Yet after so many years at sea, he pressed through the churning water, guided by experience and instinct. Exhausted from rowing and soaked to the skin, he reached the place and began calling in a trembling voice.
“Golden fish!” he shouted through the howling wind. “Golden fish!” Thunder and lightning drowned out his calls. “Golden fish!”
The fish heard him. Its shape and scales flashed once more among the towering waves. It swam around the boat for some time, then surfaced before the fisherman for the fourth time and spoke angrily:
“Did I not tell you never to return? The sea will swallow you because of your own foolishness! You let yourself be led by the nose, and it will be your ruin.”
“Dear little fish, little golden fish. For the last time, please grant my wife's request. She wishes to be a god, and no one but you can give her that.”
“After such a wish, there is only one thing left to say. When you return to land, you will find your wife back in the mud cottage. Farewell, fisherman. We shall never meet again.”
The fish dived beneath the water, leaving the fisherman alone in the storm.

Then the wind grew stronger, the waves rose higher, and the thunder roared louder. Lightning struck the water all around him. He heard the crack of breaking wood, and water began pouring into the boat. In terror, the fisherman clutched his head. There was no escape!

His beloved little boat split in two and began to sink. He fell into the raging water, which quickly closed over his head. Down he sank into the darkness of the angry sea, while beside him sank his whole life's work: his fishing boat.

When he opened his eyes again, he was lying on his back in the sand. With difficulty, he sat up and looked around. He knew this beach, this sand that offered up amber in the mornings. He knew the grassy meadows and the pines twisted by sea winds. And he recognised the mud cottage: his own home.

The door of the humble cottage opened, and his worried wife ran out. She hurried straight towards her husband, who was crawling along the beach among the wreckage of his fishing boat. She reached him and held him close with love. Then she half lifted him from the sand and led him home, exhausted and soaking wet. Ignoring the puddles of seawater he left behind, she closed the door.
Meanwhile, the sea grew calm, and the clouds slowly scattered. Sunlight began to break through them once more, telling a story of hope and a brighter tomorrow.
I don't know whether you'll agree, but few things in this world lift the spirits quite like the rays of the rising sun.
